Symphony No. 9 in D minor. Also known as the Choral Symphony, Ludwig van Beethoven's Symphony No. 9, Op. 125, completed in 1824, stands as one of the supreme achievements in human culture. It was the first symphony by a major composer to incorporate vocal soloists and a chorus, which enter in the monumental fourth movement to sing a setting of Friedrich Schiller's poem An die Freude, the Ode to Joy. Completed when Beethoven was almost entirely deaf, the symphony's scale, complexity, and humanistic message of universal brotherhood transformed the symphonic genre.

The first movement opens quietly with open fifths played tremolo in the strings, A and E, sounding like an orchestra tuning up, before exploding into a thunderous D-minor main theme. The second movement is a fast-paced scherzo, placed unusually before the slow movement. It is famous for its sudden, dramatic solo timpani octaves. The third movement is a deeply lyrical, slow movement structured as a double theme and variations. These first three movements establish the symphony's emotional and musical foundations.

The fourth movement opens with a harsh dissonance known as the horror fanfar, followed by instrumental recitatives in the cellos and basses. These instrumental passages reject the themes of the previous three movements before introducing the Ode to Joy melody. The baritone soloist sings the opening words "O Freunde, nicht diese Töne," meaning "O friends, not these tones," which Beethoven himself wrote to bridge the instrumental music to the vocal setting of Schiller's poem. A vocal quartet consisting of soprano, alto, tenor, and bass soloists joins with a full mixed chorus. The tenor soloist sings a famous military-style march version of the theme, accompanied by triangle, cymbals, and bass drum.

The premiere in Vienna was met with ecstatic applause, requiring the soloist Caroline Unger to turn the deaf composer around to witness the audience's standing ovation. The Ninth Symphony stands as a universal symbol of hope and freedom. Its melody was adapted into the official anthem of the European Union, and it was famously performed in 1989 to celebrate the fall of the Berlin Wall, where conductor Leonard Bernstein substituted the word Freiheit, meaning freedom, for Freude, meaning joy. In Japan, performing the Daiku, or Great Ninth, is an annual year-end tradition. The work influenced generations of Romantic composers, particularly Gustav Mahler and Anton Bruckner, who both inherited the model of the choral finale and shared a superstitious "curse of the ninth," the fear of dying after completing a ninth symphony.
